Do squatters have rights in Delaware?

In Delaware, someone with no permission can claim title to land only through adverse possession, and the possession has to last twenty years. A short stay in a vacant house creates no ownership, and an owner who acts early has strong options.

The words "squatter" and "adverse possession" never appear in the real actions chapter of the Delaware Code. It works through time limits instead. Title 10, chapter 79 bars a person from entering land unless within 20 years after the person's right or title first accrued, and bars a suit on prior possession unless there was actual possession within 20 years before the action. Delaware courts built the adverse possession elements on that twenty-year rule.

Two very different situations get lumped under "squatters," and the law treats them differently:

  • Long-term occupants with a claim to own: neighbors who have used a strip or a whole parcel for decades, or co-owners and heirs who stayed on in an inherited house.
  • Short-term unauthorized occupants: people who moved into a vacant home or stayed after a lease or permission ended.

What a claimant must prove

The claimant has to prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, possession that is open and notorious, hostile and adverse, exclusive, and actual, and continuous for twenty years. A Master in Chancery laid out that test in the 2020 report in Estate of Waples v. Burton.

  • Open and notorious: public enough that the owner and others are on notice. Furtive possession isn't adverse.
  • Hostile: use inconsistent with the owner's rights. The claimant needn't announce an intent to own, but must act as the owner, shutting others out.
  • Exclusive and actual: absolute exclusivity isn't required, and fences and signs aren't needed in every case.
  • Continuous for twenty years: a bright-line period, though successive possessors can add their time together (tacking) if they are in privity.

Once the claimant meets that burden, the record owner has to show by a preponderance that the use was permissive. The Delaware Supreme Court's 2004 order in Dorman v. Mitchell restated the test as possession in an "open, notorious, hostile and exclusive manner for a twenty-year period" and held that the claimant's title vested in 1991, years before the new owners learned of the property.

Permission defeats the claim. Where a landlord-tenant relationship exists, the use is permissive. In Waples, about 37 years without a rent payment was held to end a tenancy, so the facts on the ground, not labels, decide these cases.

Heirs and co-owners of an inherited house

A co-owner has a harder road. When one co-tenant claims the whole property, the claimant has to show ouster of the others, with more proof than would be needed against a stranger.

Ouster takes three things: intent, adverse possession in fact, and the other co-tenants' knowledge or notice of the adverse claim. In Waples, paying taxes and sewer charges, which began as a voluntary contribution, did not by itself show ouster. The claimant never clearly told the other co-tenants she was excluding them or claiming sole ownership, and their own use of the property was substantial. The report recommended summary judgment for the co-tenants.

For families the lesson is practical. One heir who lives in and pays for an inherited house doesn't automatically become the owner after twenty years. When heirs disagree about who owns a house, a sale can settle it. Talk to a Delaware attorney about who has authority to sell.

The 10-year disability extension

It applies sometimes. Under 10 Del. C. section 7903, a person who is an infant, mentally ill or imprisoned when the right accrues may enter or sue within 10 years after the disability ends, even if the 20-year period has run. Section 7904 gives successors in title the same benefit if the person dies while under the disability.

This matters at the edges. If title was held by a minor heir, the clock may not have run against that heir. A title company will want to know about facts like that before insuring a sale.

Removing an occupant who has no right to be there

Use the courts, not self-help. Delaware's summary possession statute, 25 Del. C. chapter 57, lets a landlord or owner file a complaint in the Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property sits. Section 5703 allows the landlord, the owner or a wrongfully excluded tenant to file.

Grounds include holdover after a lease ends, unpaid rent and lease violations. The court serves the complaint with a hearing notice, and service must happen 5 to 30 days before the hearing. When personal service fails, the court's rules provide for service by posting and mailing.

After judgment, a writ of possession issues once the appeal period passes, with at least 24 hours' notice, and execution happens between sunrise and sunset. A party can seek a new trial or review within 5 days under section 5717. Cases may be sent to mediation under the eviction diversion program in section 5702A.

The Justice of the Peace Court's instructions for a summary possession complaint call for the rental unit address, a short statement of facts, the relief sought and the filing fee. They are written for tenancies. An owner whose occupant never had a lease should talk with a Delaware attorney about the right filing.

Risk of locking someone out

If the person is a tenant, a lockout can cost the owner treble damages. Under 25 Del. C. section 5313, a tenant removed or shut out by the landlord or the landlord's agent can recover possession or end the rental agreement, and can collect three times the rent per diem for the period of exclusion, or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus court costs. The statute doesn't apply when the removal happens under a valid court order.

The occupant's status is the deciding fact. Someone who was a tenant, even briefly, may have tenant protections. The lease, rent receipts and messages help a court see what happened.

Criminal trespass is also in the Delaware Code. Third degree, section 821, covers knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on real property and is a violation. Second degree, section 822, covers a building or an enclosed property manifestly designed to exclude intruders and is an unclassified misdemeanor.

Protecting a vacant Delaware house

Regular visits and written records are the best defense against a stranger's claim. Adverse possession needs open and notorious use over twenty years, so an owner who checks the house and reacts promptly undercuts a claim long before the period runs.

  • Inspect vacant or inherited property on a schedule and keep dated notes and photos.
  • Secure doors and windows and post the owner's contact information.
  • Give written permission to any neighbor who uses a strip of the land, since permission defeats the hostile element.
  • Pay taxes and keep records of who is in the house.
  • Go to court quickly if an unauthorized occupant appears.

A vacant house with a possible occupant, back taxes or unclear heirs can be hard to sell on the open market. Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is in many situations, though a title search will show whether a claim has to be resolved first.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Delaware?

Twenty years. The possession has to be open and notorious, hostile, exclusive, actual and continuous for the whole period, and the claimant must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence.

Can paying property taxes give someone title in Delaware?

Not by itself. In Waples, a co-tenant's payment of taxes and sewer charges didn't prove ouster of the other owners. The claimant still had to show every element of adverse possession.

Does permission stop adverse possession?

Yes. Use with the owner's permission isn't hostile. Once the claimant meets the burden, the record owner has to show the use was permissive.

Can I change the locks on a person living in my Delaware house?

Not safely without a court order if the person is a tenant. Section 5313 lets a locked-out tenant recover treble damages or three times the per diem rent, whichever is greater. Talk to a Delaware attorney first.

Which Delaware court handles removal of an occupant?

The Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property sits hears summary possession cases under 25 Del. C. chapter 57. Adverse possession ownership claims have been decided in the Court of Chancery and reviewed by the Delaware Supreme Court.

Can a Delaware landlord end a tenancy because the house is being sold?

Not on that ground alone. The grounds for summary possession in 25 Del. C. 5702 do not list a sale of the property, so an owner who wants a vacant house has to use the notice rules that fit the tenancy.

Under 25 Del. C. 5106, a landlord may end a fixed-term agreement with at least 60 days' written notice before the term expires, stating that it ends on its expiration date. A month-to-month tenancy also needs 60 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the month after actual notice. An agreement that is not in writing cannot last longer than one year, and one with no stated term is treated as month-to-month.

If a lease runs a year or more and neither side gives notice at least 60 days before it ends (45 days for the tenant), section 5108 turns it into a month-to-month tenancy on the same terms. A seller who misses that window can end up with a tenant still in place at closing.

Showing a rental to buyers

A landlord must give 48 hours' notice before entering and may enter only between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. That is 25 Del. C. 5509, and it covers showings as well as repairs.

  • The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to show the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants.
  • The 48-hour notice can be waived in a signed addendum or separate signed document, for prospective tenants or purchasers only.
  • Emergencies allow entry at any time.
  • A landlord cannot use access to harass a tenant, and repeated unreasonable entry can be treated by the tenant as grounds to terminate.
  • Section 5510 makes the landlord liable for theft, casualty or other harm from entry made without the tenant's consent when the tenant is absent or present and able to consent.

Photos, lockbox visits and open houses all have to fit inside those limits.

Retaliation rules during a sale

They still apply, though a good-faith sale can be a defense. Section 5516 bars a landlord from seeking possession, raising rent or cutting services after a tenant makes a good-faith code complaint, organizes other tenants or pursues a legal remedy. It presumes retaliation when the landlord acts within 90 days.

Paragraph (d)(7) offers a defense where the landlord has in good faith contracted to sell and the contract contains a purchaser representation that the buyer will use the unit as the buyer's own residence, substantially alter or demolish it, or stop renting it for at least six months. A tenant who proves a violation can recover three months' rent or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus costs but not attorneys' fees.

If a tenant filed a repair complaint a few weeks ago, timing a notice around the sale invites a retaliation claim. Fix the complaint first, then plan the exit.

Notice for unpaid rent or a lease violation

Seven days is the minimum in both cases, under Chapters 55 and 57 of Title 25.

SituationNotice or stepSection
Unpaid rentWritten demand giving not less than 7 days before the landlord may file to terminate5502
Material lease breachWritten notice with at least 7 days to cure5513
Rent paid in full before filingLandlord may not file for possession on that ground5502(c)
Holdover after the term endsTenant owes up to double the monthly rent, prorated daily5515
Late feeCapped at 5 percent of monthly rent and not imposed within 5 days of the due date5501(d)

Section 5513 lets a landlord rely on the notice for a substantially similar breach within one year. Where a breach causes or threatens irreparable harm, the landlord may terminate on notice without the cure period.

How a Delaware eviction case works

Possession cases go to the Justice of the Peace Court. Section 5701 puts an action for summary possession in the Justice of the Peace Court that hears civil cases in the county where the rental sits.

  • The landlord files a complaint for possession, and the court serves it along with notice of the hearing time and place (section 5704).
  • After filing, section 5702A schedules the case for mediation through the court's residential eviction diversion program. Mediation must finish at least 48 hours before trial, and a tenant who fails to engage does not delay the trial.
  • Section 5704A requires lead-based paint documentation with the complaint.
  • Notices must be served personally, left with an adult at the unit, or mailed. Posting works only with a return receipt or certificate of mailing (section 5113).

Other grounds in section 5702 include holding over after the agreement ends, wrongfully deducting from rent, breaching a lawful obligation, holding over more than 5 days after a foreclosure sale with perfected title, and a sole tenant's death. Section 5115 allows an expedited forthwith summons where a tenant has caused substantial or irreparable harm.

Self-help is off the table. Section 5120 abolishes the landlord's right of distress for rent, and under section 5111 a lease clause for attorneys' fees is unenforceable.

The tenant's belongings and keys

If a landlord wins possession and there is no appeal, the landlord may remove and store the tenant's items at the tenant's expense. Seven days after the appeal period ends, the property is deemed abandoned and can be disposed of without further notice or liability (section 5507(e)).

Section 5125 covers keys. A lease cannot require surrender before the end of the term, and where there is more than one tenant, possession is returned only when all of them have complied. Document everything with photos, dates and written notices.

On the money side, a tenant's surety bond travels with the lease. Under section 5514A(j), if the landlord's interest is sold or transferred, the new landlord must accept the tenant's surety bond and may not demand an additional security deposit during the current term.

Delaware rental market basics

Rentals are a minority of Delaware housing. About 73% of occupied homes are owner-occupied, and the statewide median gross rent is $1,401. Those are statewide numbers, so a rent roll for your own building is a better guide to value.

When a rental turns into a burden, a cash buyer can purchase the house with the tenant in place or after the tenant leaves, on terms you negotiate. Have an attorney review notices and the lease first.

Preparing a rental for sale

A buyer or title company will want the lease, the payment history and every notice you have given. Collect them before listing. Write down the end date of each lease and whether it has rolled into month-to-month under section 5108, since that changes the notice a buyer must give.

Note any tenant who filed a complaint in the last 90 days and what you did about it, and keep a copy of any surety bond. If the plan is to deliver the house empty, work out the timeline from the notice period, the court steps and the stay of any appeal, and do not promise a closing date until the lease end or the court result is in hand.

Frequently asked questions

How much notice must a Delaware landlord give to end a month-to-month tenancy?

At least 60 days in writing, counted from the first day of the month after actual notice, under 25 Del. C. 5106(d). The tenant gives the same notice to end it.

How much notice does a landlord need to enter to show a rental?

At least 48 hours, and entry is allowed only between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. under 25 Del. C. 5509. Emergencies are the exception, and a tenant can sign a waiver of the 48 hours for prospective purchasers.

Where are Delaware eviction cases filed?

In the Justice of the Peace Court that hears civil cases for the county where the rental sits. After filing, the case is scheduled for mediation before trial.

Can a tenant stay if the landlord sells the house?

The sale is not listed as a ground for summary possession, so the landlord still has to end the tenancy through the lease terms and the notice rules. A buyer should ask for the lease and any notices before closing.

What if a tenant stays after the lease ends?

The tenant owes up to double the monthly rent, prorated daily, for each day of holdover under section 5515. The landlord must still use the court process to regain possession.
